claims.claim: Gen 12:1–3 records a divine call to Abram to leave country, kindred, and father's house, with a fourfold promise: a great nation, blessing, a great name, and being a blessing.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 12:1–3 read in full; Skinner pp. 240–244 (call as "trial of faith"); K&D Gen 12 (promise as ascending climax of four elements).

claims.claim: The blessing formula uses the niphal *nibrekhu* ("be blessed", passive) in Gen 12:3, against the hithpael *hitbarekhu* ("bless themselves") in Gen 22:18 and 26:4.
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 12 (niphal vs hithpael distinction, read directly); K&D Gen 22 (hithpael in the oath renewal).

claims.claim: The narrative places Abram's departure from Haran at age 75 (Gen 12:4) and Terah's death at 205 in Haran (Gen 11:32), creating the chronological tension Augustine discusses (Terah would have been 145 at the departure if Abram was born when Terah was 70).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:26, 32; 12:4 read in full; Augustine, City of God XVI.12–16 (recapitulation solution, read directly).

claims.claim: The text presents Shechem/Moreh and Bethel/Ai as Abram's first altars in Canaan (Gen 12:6–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 12:6–8 read in full.

claims.claim: "Bethel" in Gen 12:8 is proleptic: the place was still Luz at the time (the naming is recorded at Gen 28:19); K&D notes Ai ~5 miles east of Bethel (modern Beitin / Medinet Gai).
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 12 (proleptic Bethel, read directly). The Gen 28:19 cross-reference is K&D's, not independently verified this session.

claims.claim: Gen 12:10–20: famine drives Abram to Egypt; he presents Sarai as his sister; Pharaoh takes her; plagues follow; Abram is expelled with wealth.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 12:10–20 read in full; NETS 12:17 ("God tried Pharao... with great and grievous trials").

claims.claim: The wife-sister motif recurs inside this category in Gen 12 and Gen 20; Skinner reads Gen 20 as a variant of the ch. 12 tradition from a more advanced ethical standpoint (E source). A third telling, with Isaac at Gerar (Gen 26), belongs to the next category and is noted only as a forward link.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 12:10–20; 20:1–18 read in full; Skinner, Gen 20 intro (E source, advanced ethical standpoint, read directly).

claims.claim: LXX Gen 12:3 renders the blessing formula passively: "in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed", agreeing with the MT niphal.
claims.evidence: NETS Gen 12:3 read in full.

claims.claim: Skinner cites a "Field of Abram" in Sheshonk I's Karnak list (via Breasted 1904) as a possible Egyptian attestation of the Abram name, but presents it as a pointing, not a proof.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 240–244 (read directly); the identification is tentative in Skinner himself and is not corroborated by any other source read this session.

claims.claim: Gen 13: Lot chooses the Jordan plain; Abram settles in Canaan; the land promise is renewed with the command to walk through the land (13:14–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 13:1–18 read in full.

claims.claim: The text presents the separation of Abram and Lot as peaceful and initiated by Abram (13:8–9, "Let there be no strife... separate thyself, I pray thee, from me").
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 13:8–9 read in full.

claims.claim: LXX Gen 13:10 describes the Jordan plain before the overthrow as "like the orchard of God and like the land of Egypt until one came to Zogora".
claims.evidence: NETS Gen 13:10 read in full.

claims.claim: Gen 14 names four eastern kings (Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer of Elam, Tidal of Goiim) against five kings of the plain, and traces a campaign route through the Transjordan and the Negeb to Hobah, north of Damascus.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 14:1–16 read in full; NETS 14 (Amarphal, Arioch, Chodollogomor, Thargal; "salt ravine"; Choba left of Damascus).

claims.claim: Skinner judges the four royal names historical and "some such expedition" possibly historical, but the campaign details unattested; the chapter is an idealisation — "a Bedouin razzia magnified into a systematic campaign".
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. ~271–276 (read directly). A scholarly judgment, contested in the literature; the historicity debate is second-hand in this dossier (§7.3).

claims.claim: The assumption that the vale of Siddim became the Dead Sea is erroneous on geological evidence: the depression predates human habitation (Skinner).
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 14 (read directly). A geological claim as reported by Skinner, not independently verified this session.

claims.claim: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of El Elyon, brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tithe of all (Gen 14:18–20); LXX: "priest of God Most High".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 14:18–20; NETS 14:18–20 read in full; Josephus Ant. 1.10 (Melchizedek "righteous King", priest of God, Salem → Jerusalem; tithe).

claims.claim: *El Elyon* ("God Most High") first occurs in Genesis in Gen 14 (BDB H5945); the title is attached to Melchizedek's priesthood and to Abram's oath (14:22).
claims.evidence: BDB H5945 (read directly); KJV Gen 14:18–22.

claims.claim: Gen 15 divides into two parts: the promise of a son (vv. 1–6) and the promise of the land (vv. 7–21); the covenant strictly embraces the land (Skinner).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 15:1–21; Skinner, Gen 15 intro (read directly); K&D Gen 15 (whole chapter as vision; covenant as spiritual fellowship).

claims.claim: Gen 15:6 — "he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness"; LXX: "Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 15:6; NETS 15:6 read in full.

claims.claim: The covenant ritual of Gen 15 (divided heifer, she-goat, ram, turtledove, pigeon; a smoking furnace and burning torch passing between the pieces, 15:17) is described in the text as a theophanic act accompanying the land grant "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates" (15:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 15:9–18 read in full; NETS 15:17–18.

claims.claim: The cutting ceremony follows a known ancient covenant custom (cf. Jer 34:18, the parties passing between the halves of a calf); K&D, citing Ephraem Syrus, notes God followed "the custom of the Chaldeans" in the manner of covenant-making.
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 15 (read directly). The Jer 34:18 parallel is K&D's; Jer 34 was not read in full this session (range verified via API for conn-ab-014).

claims.claim: Jubilees 14 retells the Gen 15 covenant as a dream vision: Abram sacrifices the animals and pours the blood on the altar; a horror of great darkness falls; a smoking furnace and a flame of fire pass between the pieces; the covenant is made that day and dated to the 15th of Sivan, renewing the covenant made with Noah.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 14 read in full (Charles, sacred-texts).

claims.claim: Gen 15:13's "four hundred years" of sojourning and affliction is read by Josephus as 400 years in Egypt (Ant. 1.10); the text itself says the seed will be "a stranger in a land that is not theirs", and the figure's exact referent (Egypt alone vs the whole sojourn) is disputed.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 15:13; Josephus Ant. 1.10 (400 years in Egypt, read directly). The dispute is a standard interpretive disagreement; the dossier does not resolve it.

claims.claim: Gen 17 presents circumcision as the sign/token of the covenant, on the eighth day, extended to every male of the household including slaves, with "cut off" as the penalty for the uncircumcised (17:9–14, 23–27).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 17:9–14, 23–27; Skinner pp. 295–298 (circumcision as covenant-sign/token; 8th day; slaves included; "cut off" unresolved between death and excommunication); K&D Gen 17 (circumcision as symbol of heart-circumcision).

claims.claim: In P, circumcision becomes a first-magnitude prescription, second only to the Sabbath; Skinner holds the rite was originally a puberty initiation, evidenced by Old Kingdom wall-pictures at Sakkara showing the operation with flint knives.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 295–298 (read directly). A historical reconstruction by Skinner, not independently verified this session.

claims.claim: On P's covenant-idea Skinner takes a middle position between Valeton (unilateral divine self-obligation) and Kraetzschmar (bilateral engagement): an immutable determination of God's purpose carrying conditions whose neglect excludes the individual.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 295–298, "The Covenant-idea in P" (read directly). A scholarly reconstruction, reported as Skinner's position.

claims.claim: *El Shadday*: K&D derives it from *shadad*, "to be strong"; BDB records the etymology as dubious — rabbinic *she* + *day* ("self-sufficient"), *shadad* ("almighty"), or conjectured *sheday* ("my sovereign lord").
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 17 (read directly); BDB H7706 (read directly).

claims.claim: Abraham's laughter in Gen 17:17 is joyous amazement, not unbelief (Delitzsch, Calvin, via K&D); his plea "O that Ishmael might live before thee" (17:18) expresses anxiety lest Ishmael have no part in the covenant.
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 17 (read directly). An interpretive judgment reported via K&D.

claims.claim: The covenant is established with Isaac alone (Gen 17:19, 21) while Ishmael is separately blessed: twelve princes, a great nation (17:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 17:19–21 read in full; NETS 17:19–21.

claims.claim: Gen 16: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram; Hagar conceives and despises her mistress; Sarai afflicts her; Hagar flees; the Angel of the LORD meets her at the spring on the way to Shur, sends her back with a promise of numerous offspring, and names the child Ishmael.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 16:1–16 read in full; NETS 16 (Sara "maltreated her"; spring "on the way to Sour"; "I will multitudinously multiply your offspring").

claims.claim: The Hagar narrative is the oldest stratum of Gen 16; J and E variants exist for the flight and the theophany (Skinner).
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 16 (read directly). A source-critical judgment, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: The surrogacy arrangement parallels Hammurabi §146 (a slave-girl given to the husband to bear children; Skinner). Hammurabi §146 itself was not opened in full this session.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 16 (read directly, citing §146). The registry's Hammurabi entry notes §146 was consulted only via search-result text.

claims.claim: Ishmael's name means "God hears" (Gen 16:11, "because the LORD hath heard thy affliction"); LXX 16:12 renders the prophecy "He shall be a rustic man" for MT "a wild ass of a man"; Josephus glosses the name as "Heard of God" (Ant. 1.10).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 16:11–12; NETS 16:11–12; Josephus Ant. 1.10 (read directly).

claims.claim: Hagar names God El-roi, "Thou God seest me" (Gen 16:13); LXX: "You-are-the-God-who-looks-upon-me"; the well is Beer-lahai-roi, "between Kadesh and Bered" (MT) / "between Kades and Barad" (LXX).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 16:13–14; NETS 16:13–14 read in full.

claims.claim: Gen 21:9–21: Sarah sees Ishmael "mocking" (KJV) / "playing with her son Isaak" (LXX); demands the expulsion; God confirms it but promises to make Ishmael a great nation; Hagar and Ishmael are sent away with bread and a bottle of water; God opens her eyes to a well; Ishmael grows up in the wilderness of Paran, becomes an archer, and marries an Egyptian wife.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 21:9–21; NETS 21:9–21 read in full.

claims.claim: The narrative gives Ishmael's birth when Abram was 86 (Gen 16:16) and Isaac's when Abraham was 100 (Gen 21:5), yet Gen 21:14–16 portrays Ishmael as a child put on Hagar's shoulder, cast under a shrub, and wept over as dying — a tension between the chronological data and the scene's staging.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 16:16; 21:5, 14–16 read in full. The data are textual; the tension is noted, not resolved (DQ-06).

claims.claim: Josephus reports that Arabs circumcise after the thirteenth year because Ishmael was circumcised at thirteen (Ant. 1.12).
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 1.12 (read directly).

claims.claim: Ishmael's twelve sons (Gen 25:13–15) are presented as twelve princes/tribes; Skinner reads them as a confederacy, identifies Nabayoth/Kedar with the Nabayati/Aidri of Assyrian records, and doubts the Nabataean identification.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 25:1–18 (read directly). Assyrian identifications are Skinner's, not independently verified this session.

claims.claim: Gen 18: three visitors at Mamre; Sarah's laughter at the announcement of a son within the year; the promise "I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life" (18:10, 14).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 18:1–15 read in full; NETS 18:10–14 ("Can it be that a matter is impossible with God?").

claims.claim: Gen 18:17–19: God will not hide from Abraham what he is about to do, because Abraham "shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him", and because he will command his children and household to keep the way of the LORD, doing righteousness and justice.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 18:17–19; NETS 18:17–19 read in full.

claims.claim: Abraham's intercession (Gen 18:23–32) bargains from fifty righteous down to ten; LXX 18:25: "Shall not you, the one who judges all the earth, do what is just?"
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 18:23–32; NETS 18:23–32 read in full.

claims.claim: The Bible Odyssey "Sodom and Gomorrah" article reads the story in a seven-visit structure, notes this is the first time Abraham initiates conversation with God, and takes hospitality vs inhospitality as the story's point.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "Sodom and Gomorrah" (read in full). An interpretive reading by the article, reported as such.

claims.claim: Gen 19: two angels come to Sodom; Lot's hospitality; the men of the city demand the visitors; Lot offers his daughters; the angels blind the attackers; Lot's family is urged out; his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt; brimstone and fire rain from the LORD out of heaven.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 19:1–29 read in full; NETS 19 (19:24 "sulfur and fire from the Lord out of the sky"; 19:26 "stele of salt"; 19:29 "God remembered Abraam and sent Lot out").

claims.claim: LXX Gen 19:24 preserves the double "Lord" phrasing: "the Lord rained on Sodoma and Gomorra sulfur and fire from the Lord out of the sky".
claims.evidence: NETS Gen 19:24 read in full.

claims.claim: Josephus reports Lot's wife's pillar of salt as still visible in his day — "I have seen it" — and glosses Zoar as "small thing" (Ant. 1.11).
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 1.11 (read directly).

claims.claim: Gen 19:30–38: Lot's daughters, believing mankind destroyed, bear Moab ("from my father") and Ben-ammi ("son of my people/race"); LXX 19:37–38 gives the same etymologies (Moab "From my father", Amman "Son of my race").
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 19:30–38; NETS 19:37–38 read in full.

claims.claim: Skinner reads Gen 19:30–38 as a pendant to the Sodom story, parallel in function to Noah's drunkenness as an appendix to the Flood, expressing national hatred and contempt for Moab and Ammon.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 19:30–38 (read directly). An interpretive judgment, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: Gunkel's theory (via Skinner): the Lot's-daughters episode was originally a Moabite legend — Lot worshipped at the cave; the daughters' act presupposes a universal catastrophe; Lot functions as a counterpart of Noah.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 19:30–38, reporting Gunkel (read directly in Skinner). Second-hand for Gunkel himself.

claims.claim: Gen 20: Abimelech of Gerar takes Sarah; God warns him in a dream; Abimelech protests his innocence; Abraham explains "she is my sister" (daughter of his father, not his mother, 20:12); Abraham is called a prophet who will pray for Abimelech (20:7); Abimelech restores Sarah with gifts.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 20:1–18 read in full; NETS 20 (20:7 "he is a prophet"; 20:12 "my sister by my father, but not by my mother"; 20:16 "a thousand didrachmas... for the honor of your person").

claims.claim: Skinner: Gen 20 is a variant of the ch. 12 wife-sister tradition from a more advanced ethical standpoint (E source); Abimelech is a genuine Canaanite name (cf. Amarna Tablets 149–156, the governor of Tyre); Gerar was an independent Canaanite kingdom, with no Philistine anachronism in this chapter.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 20 intro (read directly). The Amarna citation is Skinner's, not independently verified this session.

claims.claim: The Bible Odyssey "Sarah, Abraham, and Pharaoh" article argues the sister was perceived as sexually available, so there was no reason to kill the brother; the patriarch is rebuked in all three wife-sister episodes; household and community are endangered.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "Sarah, Abraham, and Pharaoh" (read in full). An interpretive reading by the article.

claims.claim: Gen 22:1–19: God tests Abraham — "take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest"; the journey to Moriah; Isaac carries the wood; "God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering" (22:8); the binding; the angel's intervention; the ram substituted; the place named Jehovah-jireh; the oath renewal of the promise (22:15–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 22:1–19 read in full; NETS 22 (22:2 "the high land"; 22:5 "we will come back to you"; 22:9 "bound his son Isaak hand and foot"; 22:12 "For now I know that you do fear God"; 22:14 "The Lord saw").

claims.claim: *ʿāqad* (H6123, "bind") occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible, Gen 22:9 — hence the event's traditional name, the Akedah, "the Binding".
claims.evidence: BDB H6123 (read directly).

claims.claim: "God tempted Abraham" (KJV 22:1) means tested/proved; Augustine reads temptation as probation — to make Abraham's faith known to the world, not to God — and "Now I know" (22:12) as "Now I have made to be known" (City of God XVI.32).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 22:1, 12; Augustine XVI.32 (read directly).

claims.claim: Moriah: "All attempts to explain the name and identify the place have been futile" (Skinner); the Temple-mount tradition (Jubilees 18, 2 Chr 3:1, Josephus Ant. 1.224) is late and unreliable (Skinner). The LXX does not transliterate the name at all: "go into the high land" (NETS 22:2).
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 22 intro (read directly); NETS 22:2. A negative scholarly judgment, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: Josephus: Isaac was 25 years old; Moriah is the mountain where David built the temple; Isaac consents willingly to the sacrifice; God tested "the temper of his mind", not desiring human blood (Ant. 1.13).
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 1.13 (read directly).

claims.claim: Philo, *De Abrahamo* §§167–177: the Akedah is "the most important action of all... of more importance than all the actions of piety and religion put together"; the interrupted sacrifice is "recorded and engraved as a complete and perfect sacrifice" (§177).
claims.evidence: Philo, De Abr. §§167–177 (read directly, Yonge/Colson via earlyjewishwritings).

claims.claim: Philo, *De Abrahamo* §§178–188: against critics who note that pagans sacrifice children, Abraham's act differs because others sacrifice from custom, fear, or desire for glory, while his was voluntary, from love of God alone.
claims.evidence: Philo, De Abr. §§178–188 (read directly).

claims.claim: Jubilees 17:15–18: the prince Mastema proposes the test; Abraham has already passed six trials (his land, the famine, the wealth of kings, his wife taken, circumcision, sending away Hagar and Ishmael); Jubilees 18 retells the binding and institutes a seven-day festival.
claims.evidence: Second-hand via search excerpts (Charles text as reproduced; Fitzmyer 2002 summary; docslib chapter on Jub. 17:15–18:19). Jub 17–18 NOT read directly this session; Jub 14 was read in full (clm-ab-022).

claims.claim: Augustine XVI.32: Abraham believed Isaac would rise again (Heb 11:19); the ram caught by the horns prefigures Jesus crowned with thorns; Isaac carrying the wood prefigures Christ carrying his cross; the oath is unique — God had often promised but never sworn.
claims.evidence: Augustine XVI.32 (read directly). The Heb 11:19 reference is Augustine's.

claims.claim: Chrysostom, Homily 47 on Gen 22 (second-hand): "Take your beloved son Isaac, whom you dearly love" kindles the fire of the father's agony; "God Himself will see to a sheep for a burnt offering, my child" unwittingly foretells what was to happen. Homily 48: "It was more atrocious for a father to slay a son than to be slain." The ten testings tradition counts the Akedah the gravest.
claims.evidence: Second-hand via quoted excerpts only; Hom. 47–48 NOT read directly (FOTC Hill translation not freely available).

claims.claim: Gunkel's cult-legend theory of the Akedah (via Skinner): the story originated as a cult legend explaining the substitution of animal for human sacrifice; parallels cited are Phoenician Kronos and Iphigeneia.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 22 end, reporting Gunkel (read directly in Skinner). Second-hand for Gunkel himself.

claims.claim: K&D Gen 22: the trial purifies love; "Ha-Elohim" is distinguished from Jehovah; Moriah is "shown of Jehovah"; the oath is unique in patriarchal intercourse; "we will come again" (22:5); Isaac's silent submission; the animal substituted for the human; the prophetic importance runs Moriah → temple → Christ.
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 22 (read directly). A theological interpretation, reported as K&D's.

claims.claim: Gen 23: Sarah dies at 127 in Kirjath-arba (Hebron); Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite for 400 shekels of silver, in the presence of the sons of Heth — the first landed possession in Canaan.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 23:1–20 read in full; NETS 23 (23:1 "one hundred twenty-seven years"; 23:2 "city of Arbok... (this is Chebron)"; 23:6 "a king from a god among us"; 23:15–16 "four hundred didrachmas of silver certified by merchants").

claims.claim: Skinner Gen 23: the chapter is P source, secular in tone, a local (Hebron) tradition; Sayce's Babylonian-contract argument is refuted; the "Hittites" in the south are questioned; "Hittite" in P is a general designation.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 23 (read directly). Scholarly judgments, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: Gen 24: Abraham sends his servant to Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac; the thigh oath (24:2–3, 9); the sign at the well; Rebekah's consent ("I will go", 24:58); Isaac marries her and "was comforted after his mother's death" (24:67). The servant is unnamed in the chapter; the traditional identification with Eliezer rests on Gen 15:2.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 24:1–67 read in full; NETS 24 (24:6 "do not bring my son back there"; 24:10 "Mesopotamia to the city of Nachor"; 24:27 "righteousness and truth"; 24:62 "well of the appearance").

claims.claim: Skinner Gen 24: two narratives (J+E) combined; the thigh oath; Aram Naharaim = Egyptian Naharin; the Bethuel gloss; the death of Abraham suppressed by the Redactor (the chapter's chronology implies Abraham still alive).
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 24 (read directly). Source-critical judgments, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: Gen 25:1–6: Abraham takes Keturah; six sons (Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, Shuah); he gives all that he has to Isaac and sends the sons of the concubines eastward with gifts while still living.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 25:1–6; NETS 25:1–6 read in full; Josephus Ant. 1.15 (Keturah's six sons; Ophren → Africa via Alexander Polyhistor/Cleodemus Malchus).

claims.claim: Skinner: Keturah is possibly a variant of Hagar; Midian lies in the north Hijaz; "gathered to his kindred" (25:8) is Sheol language; P ignores the expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael.
claims.evidence: Skinner, Gen 25:1–18 (read directly). Scholarly judgments, reported as Skinner's.

claims.claim: Gen 25:7–11: Abraham dies at 175, "gathered to his people"; Isaac and Ishmael bury him in Machpelah with Sarah; God blesses Isaac, who settles by Beer-lahai-roi.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 25:7–11; NETS 25:7–11 read in full; Josephus Ant. 1.17 (died 175, buried Hebron with Sarah by Isaac and Ishmael); Augustine XVI.34 (died 175, Isaac 75).

claims.claim: Gen 25:12–18: Ishmael's twelve sons are named (Nebajoth, Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadar, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, Kedemah); he lives 137 years; his settlements stretch "from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria", dwelling "in the presence of all his brethren" (KJV) / LXX "he settled facing all his kinfolk".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 25:12–18; NETS 25:12–18 read in full; Josephus Ant. 1.12 (the twelve sons named; inhabited from the Euphrates to the Red Sea, "Nabatene").

claims.claim: The genealogy of Gen 11:10–26 (Shem to Terah) functions as the bridge from the primeval history to Abraham; Gen 12:1 follows it directly, and Stephen's speech (Acts 7:2–4) places the call in Mesopotamia before the dwelling in Haran.
claims.evidence: NETS Gen 11:10–26 (read in full in the NETS Gen 12–25 read); KJV Gen 12:1; Augustine XVI.12–16 (Acts 7:2–3, read directly). The Acts 7:2–4 range is verified via API (Acts 7 has 60 verses) and the content is Augustine's citation, not an independent read of Acts.

connections.note: The Shem → Terah genealogy is the entry bridge from the primeval history into Abraham. Belongs by subject to the Nations and Babel category; used here only as the handover.

The Noahic covenant (with all flesh; sign of the bow) is the background against which the Abrahamic covenant (with one man and his seed; signs of the cut animals and circumcision) is read. Same covenant vocabulary, different parties and signs. Not duplicated from the SC event.
"God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob" — the Exodus deliverance is presented as the fulfilment of the Gen 15 promise.
"I have also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan" — the covenant formula restated at the Exodus.
The eighth-day circumcision ordinance in the Law, carrying forward the Gen 17 sign.
"The faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him... to a thousand generations" — the everlasting covenant remembered.

"Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah... and they served other gods. And I took your father Abraham from the other side of the flood" — the only OT passage that states the family's prior polytheism outright.
"Kings shall come out of thee" (Gen 17:6) fulfilled in the Davidic covenant; the promise of a great name and an everlasting house.

"Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham; and madest a covenant with him" — the post-exilic retelling of the call and covenant.

"O ye seed of Abraham his servant... He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations. Which covenant he made with Abraham... Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan."
"The princes of the people are gathered together, even the people of the God of Abraham" — the nations gathered to Abraham's God.
"Thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend" — the only OT passage calling Abraham God's friend.
"Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him."
The new covenant ("I will be their God, and they shall be my people", 31:33) reuses the Gen 17 covenant formula ("to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee", 17:7).
The parties who "passed between the parts" of the cut calf — the only other biblical description of the Gen 15 cutting ceremony, and K&D's evidence for the custom (clm-ab-021).

"I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine" — covenant-and-oath language echoing Gen 15/17, addressed to Jerusalem. Thematic, not a direct Abraham reference.
"Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old" — *ḥesed* to Abraham (BDB H2617 II.1.e).
"The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begat Isaac" — the NT genealogy opens with Abraham.
"God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham" — descent from Abraham is no guarantee; the promise is not a birthright. Parallel passages, one connection. (Parallel: Luke 3:8.)
"Abraham's bosom" (16:22) — Abraham as the resting place of the righteous dead in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus.
"Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad... Before Abraham was, I am" (8:56, 58) — the sharpest NT claim about Abraham's relation to Christ.

"Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed" — Peter quotes the promise as the covenant's content.

Stephen's retelling: the call in Mesopotamia before Haran; the sojourn; the 400 years; the covenant of circumcision. The earliest witness to the recapitulation reading of the Terah chronology (clm-ab-003).

"Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness" (4:3, quoting Gen 15:6); "a father of many nations" (4:17–18, quoting Gen 17:5). The fullest NT exposition of the promise by faith.
"In Isaac shall thy seed be called... At this time will I come, and Sara shall have a son" — Paul on the election of Isaac over Ishmael.

"In thee shall all nations be blessed" (3:8, quoting Gen 12:3); "he saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ" (3:16); "if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed" (3:29). (Exact verses: Gal 3:6–18, 29.)
The Hagar/Sarah allegory: "these are the two covenants" (4:24); "Cast out the bondwoman and her son" (4:30, quoting Gen 21:10). A NT reception, not a claim about the Genesis text's own meaning.
"When God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself" — the oath of Gen 22 as the anchor of hope.
Melchizedek, "king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him... to whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all".

"By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out... obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went" (11:8); "accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead" (11:19, on the binding).

"Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?... And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God."
"Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord" — the only NT reference to Sarah's speech to Abraham ("my lord", Gen 18:12).

"Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire."
